title: Chapter L

teacherSummary.text: Elizabeth realizes Darcy is the man who would have suited her best, just as she believes the family disgrace has ended her chances. Wickham is to join the regulars in the north.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “instead of spending his whole income, he had laid by an annual sum, for the better provision of his children” slowly and put it in my own words: Mr. Bennet now wishes he had saved part of his income each year for his children. Next, craft. I notice the calm narration of a regret that comes too late. The strongest word is “provision”: it means planning for the future, which he never did. Then, effect. What does Mr. Bennet regret? My answer: Mr. Bennet regrets that he never saved part of his income for his children; his carelessness left his daughters unprotected, and now another man has paid to save the family, which humbles him.

followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?

items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: Elizabeth recognizes her love for Darcy just when circumstances seem to forbid it. Useful evidence: “But no such happy marriage could now teach the admiring multitude what connubial felicity really was” (Chapter L, paragraph 16): The narrator's gently ironic picture of the lost ideal. Theme link: the cost of Mr. Bennet's carelessness becomes concrete. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the chapter to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
